title: Knowing that binds
hookLine: the second Shiva Sutra says knowledge is bondage, and a lover who goes unrecognized shows why
carry: knowledge binds when it says i am only this
tomorrow: why would wonder be a sign of the path?

cards: Knowledge is bondage. That's the whole second line of the Shiva Sutras, two words in Sanskrit: jnanam bandhah.

Read it cold and it sounds like an attack on school, on books, on curiosity, on everything a library stands for. It isn't. But it's meant to stop you, the way a do-not-enter sign makes you look twice at the door.
The first thread said consciousness is the self. This one says what goes wrong.

teach.b: Consciousness is the self, and in this tradition that consciousness is Shiva's own: wide, free, whole. So why does a person feel so small? The second thread answers: knowing binds.
Commentators read knowledge here as limited knowing: the quiet, constant sense of I am only this.
Only this body, this anxious person, this bad grade. Not wrong information, but too small a picture of who's doing the knowing.

Kshemaraja's commentary ties it to the tradition's impurities, starting with anava mala, the stain of smallness. Then a later teacher of the same Kashmir tradition, Utpaladeva, tells a little story to show the way out.
A young woman has fallen in love with a man she has only heard about.
She longs for him. One day he's standing right in front of her, and she feels nothing, because she doesn't know it's him.
Then someone tells her: that's him. Nothing about him changes. But now her joy is complete.
That, Utpaladeva says, is how it is with us and the Lord. Shiva is already here, as our own awareness, and the small knowing keeps us from seeing it.

So freedom isn't getting something new. It's recognition, pratyabhijna, a word that gives a whole school in Kashmir its name. On an ordinary day, the small knowing sounds like I'm just bad at this, or I always mess up.
A label that started as information and became a wall. The second thread doesn't ask you to stop knowing things. It asks who you think is doing the knowing.

how: Students of Kashmir Shaivism read the Shiva Sutras slowly with a commentary, and the tradition's teachers describe freedom as recognition (pratyabhijna) of one's own nature as Shiva.

o: Shiva teaching from Kashmir: small knowing is what binds
a rule that monks must forget everything they've learned
a Kashmir school that warns students against reading books

games.q: the second thread — tap the pairs.

s: the second sutra is against books and learning
commentators read it as limited knowing: the sense of I am only this.
in this teaching, freedom is also a kind of knowing
not a new fact but a recognition: consciousness seeing itself whole.
in Utpaladeva's story, the lover changes so she can love him
nothing about him changes; she only recognizes him, and her joy is complete.

games.q: you read a sacred line: knowledge is bondage. what do you do with it?
o: ask what kind of knowing binds.
decide the line must be a mistake.
games.why: the commentators ask exactly that: the knowing that binds is the limited sense of I am only this.

practice: Let a sentence come up that starts with I'm just, or I'm only, or I always, something you say about yourself, and hold it gently.
On each out-breath, let the space around it grow wider, the way the woman's whole view changed when she knew who was standing there; the label can stay, it just isn't the whole room anymore.
If you pray, you can say softly: you were here all along. If you don't, rest in the first thread, consciousness is the self.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir Shaivism opening. The second thread of the Shiva Sutras: jnanam bandhah, knowledge is bondage, the small knowing that says I am only this.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shiva Sutra 1.2, knowledge (jnanam) is bondage (bandhah).

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge binds when it says I am only this. The way out is recognition, not something new. Until tomorrow.
